# Discourse Report, Part D — Legal, Philosophical, and Privacy-Scholarship Strata

*The Governable Mind*, draft v1 (`drafts/v1.md`). Written 2026-09-16, progressively. Line numbers refer to `drafts/v1.md`. Every source cited here was fetched and read on 2026-09-16 unless marked "(abstract/secondary only)"; source notes live in `agents/editor/research/sources/` and are indexed in `agents/editor/research/index-partD.md`. A parallel report covers the AI-policy / open-weights / compute-governance discourse; this one does not duplicate it.

Sections are ordered as requested by the coordinator's priority list, then renumbered at the end to the brief's scheme: (6) live legal record; (4) third-party doctrine; (1) predecessors; (3) uncited work; (4′) strongest counterargument; (2) originality verdict; (5) misrepresentation check; (7) reception.

---

## 6. The live legal record on chat logs (2025–2026), with dates and sources

**Bottom line for the editor.** The cognitive record is not a forecast. Between May 2025 and June 2026 it became a preserved, sampled, subpoenaed, warranted, and adjudicated object in US federal courts, and a US Supreme Court decision (June 29, 2026) narrowed the very doctrine that would have left it unprotected. The draft's "anticipatory rather than accusatory" framing at l.20 and its "As of this writing no liberal state has built the architecture" sentence are defensible only on the narrow reading (no *state* has built *identity-gated inference, attested hardware, signed weights, mandatory searchable memory*). On the broader reading a legally literate reader will take from l.88–92 — that the searchability of the record of deliberation is a thing to be feared in prospect — the draft undersells its own case by roughly a year. The chronology:

| Date | Event | What it establishes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|

OpenAI / Microsoft*, orders OpenAI to "preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted on a going forward basis," including chats users had deleted and Temporary Chats. Enterprise and zero-data-retention API customers exempt. | A private litigant, not a state, made *every consumer's* deletion inoperative for four months. The mechanism the draft calls "durable and searchable memory because the safety systems need it" (l.286) arrived first as civil-discovery preservation. | Engadget, Oct. 23, 2025, https://www.engadget.com/ai/openai-no-longer-has-to-preserve-all-of-its-chatgpt-data-with-some-exceptions-192422093.html ; Simon Willison, Oct. 23, 2025, https://simonwillison.net/2025/Oct/23/openai-no-longer-has-to-preserve/ (OpenAI's own explainer at https://openai.com/index/response-to-nyt-data-demands/ returned 403 to me; cited via the secondary reports). |

**Answer to the editor's question.** Yes: the cognitive record is already a litigated, warranted, and sampled object, and the draft's "anticipatory" framing undersells its case. But the *specific* architecture the draft fears — state-mandated identity, attestation, signed weights, searchable memory — has not been built by any liberal state; what exists is (a) ordinary civil and criminal process reaching a record the provider already keeps, (b) provider-side scanning and referral, (c) a legislative pipeline for identity verification. That is precisely the draft's own layer-3 point at l.244 ("the easiest to enforce because the provider already holds the record"). The fix is not to abandon "anticipatory" but to split it: the *record* is present-tense (cite the table above in §III at l.88–92 and in §XI at l.232); the *architecture* is prospective (keep l.20 and l.294). The draft's §XIII sentence "A provider that answers a lawful subpoena does not constitute it" (l.276) is right, but it now needs the companion sentence: twenty million conversations were produced under such process in January 2026, so "lawful subpoena" is no longer a limiting case.

Two further facts the author should weigh. First, *Heppner* turned on the provider's retention and training terms; a locally run model would have produced no third-party record at all, which is the strongest concrete illustration of "epistemic exit" (l.120) available in the record, and the draft does not use it. Second, the Palisades-fire indictment used a ChatGPT question — a *hypothetical* ("are you at fault if…") — as evidence of state of mind; that is the draft's §III claim about "the developmental history of a belief" (l.88) instantiated in a charging document.

## 4. The third-party doctrine

**What the draft omits.** Nowhere in v1 does the phrase "third-party doctrine," *Smith v. Maryland* (1979), *United States v. Miller* (1976), or *Carpenter v. United States* (2018) appear. Yet the draft's central legal move — that protection attaches to the *medium* of deliberation, "letters, reading lists, library records" (l.86) — runs straight into the one US doctrine that says information "voluntarily turned over to third parties" carries no reasonable expectation of privacy, and the draft's layer 3 (hosted inference, l.232) is by definition a third-party record. The prior essay (*The Politics of Visibility*) cited *Carpenter* and *Chatrie*; this one, written a month later, cites neither, and the author's legally literate readers will notice the regression.

**State of the doctrine as applied to chat logs (fetched sources).**
- CRS LSB11429 (May 5, 2026): the applicability of the Fourth Amendment to chatbot histories "may hinge in large part on the limits of the third-party doctrine"; *Carpenter* was "narrow" and "did not abolish the third-party doctrine or predetermine its application to other forms of technological surveillance"; no federal court has yet decided the question; in practice law enforcement uses SCA § 2703 warrants (which is why the question rarely reaches a court). https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/LSB/PDF/LSB11429/LSB11429.1.pdf
- *Chatrie* (June 29, 2026): data "held by a third party" does not by itself take location history outside the Fourth Amendment; the Court reasoned from *Carpenter*'s two prongs — indispensability and revealing character. Both prongs are arguable for chat logs; the IAPP panel (May 2026) argued exactly that. https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/07/supreme-court-holds-geofence-warrant-access ; https://www.ashurstperkinscoie.com/en/insights/old-doctrines-new-terrain-the-fourth-amendment-the-stored-communications-act-and-law-enforcement-dem/
- *NYT v. OpenAI* (Stein, J., Jan. 2026): the voluntary-submission logic was applied, in a civil-discovery posture, to reject the privacy objection to producing 20 million logs. https://natlawreview.com/article/openai-loses-privacy-gambit-20-million-chatgpt-logs-likely-headed-copyright
- *Heppner* (Feb. 2026) and Kumar's HLR critique: Rakoff treated the platform's data terms as destroying confidentiality; Kumar replies that courts treat software tools (Gmail, Google Docs, iCloud) as not breaking privilege and invokes *Katz*'s subjective-plus-reasonable expectation. https://harvardlawreview.org/blog/2026/03/united-states-v-heppner/
- Richards's 2008 "Intellectual Privacy" (which the draft cites) discusses the doctrine's consequences for reading records (I could not fetch the full text today to confirm page cites; the 2015 book's chapters "Reading" and "Confiding" are the standard treatment).

**Assessment.** For a general reader the omission is invisible. For the legally literate reader the draft explicitly claims (brief §"Intended audience": "legally literate since *The Politics of Visibility*"), it is the largest gap in the piece, and it is a gap in the *argument*, not only the citations: the draft's diary analogy (l.84) works in the toleration tradition because the diary was in the writer's desk; the cognitive record is in the provider's datacenter, and US law has for fifty years treated that difference as dispositive. The remedy is short — two or three sentences in §III after l.86 or in §XI at l.232 — and it strengthens the essay: *Carpenter* and *Chatrie* show the doctrine bending toward "indispensable and revealing" media, which is the draft's own description of the externalized forum internum. The draft can say: the law is already deciding whether the medium of deliberation is a bank record or a home, and it is deciding it case by case, in warrants that never reach an appellate court.

One more point against interest: because the draft's structural argument locates the danger at layer 3–4 *by design* (l.244) and not in any specific doctrine, its analysis survives even if *Chatrie* eventually extends to chat logs. A warrant requirement governs *access*; it does not touch *retention*, *classification*, or *referral*, which is where the draft's four conditions (l.272) live. That is a real advantage over the privacy-law literature, which is almost entirely about the access question, and the draft should claim it.

## 1. Predecessors and neighbors on cognitive liberty and freedom of thought

Per source: what it claimed; where the draft agrees, extends, or diverges; URL. Ordered by importance to the draft, not chronology.

### 1.1 Marc Jonathan Blitz, "Freedom of Thought for the Extended Mind: Cognitive Enhancement and the Constitution," 2010 Wis. L. Rev. 1049–1118 — **the direct predecessor the draft does not know it has**
- **Claim.** Read in full (OKCU repository PDF, https://scholarship.law.okcu.edu/downloads/d7kcg-2ck33/fulltext.pdf). Blitz argues that constitutional freedom of thought "cannot and should not protect all activity that arises from or influences thought, but rather activity that is either (1) the functional equivalent of thought, or (2) a reshaping of the self that does that thinking" (p. 1073). He builds the case from the diary: journal-writing is protected "not based only on freedom of speech, but freedom of the thinking that underlies it"; Orwell's Winston begins his rebellion "with an entry in a diary" (p. 1068–69); then asks "if Otto receives First Amendment protection when he inscribes the information he perceives into a journal, why not give him the same protection when he records it in a brain chip"; the category includes "someone's regular and automatic use of a journal or iPhone to recall information" (p. 1075). He cites *Baumgartner v. United States* (1944) refusing to use pro-Nazi diary entries against a citizen.
- **Relation to the draft.** This is the draft's §III move — the diary analogy (l.84), "protection attaches to media" (l.86), the functional definition of the externalized forum internum (l.82) — made sixteen years earlier, in US constitutional terms, explicitly on Clark & Chalmers, and with a limiting principle. The draft *diverges* usefully: Blitz's concern is the state *forbidding* cognitive tools (enhancement drugs, chips); the draft's is the state *reading and permissioning* them. Blitz has no surveillance argument, no chilling literature, no political-economy of chokepoints. The draft extends Blitz from the liberty to use the tool to the liberty to use it unobserved. It should say so, in one sentence, and cite him — not least because Blitz co-edits the Palgrave *Law and Ethics of Freedom of Thought* volumes the draft already cites at [17], and Bublitz's 2013 chapter (below) attacks Blitz's move by name. A neurorights reader will assume the author read the footnote and stayed silent.
- **Verdict on the "externalized forum internum" move:** *unwitting reinvention* of Blitz 2010's "functional equivalent of thought," with a genuine extension (observation and permission rather than prohibition; the developmental record rather than the stored fact).

### 1.2 Jan Christoph Bublitz, "My Mind is Mine!? Cognitive Liberty as a Legal Concept" (2013), and the 2021/2025 papers
- **Claim (2013, read in full: https://www.antoniocasella.eu/dnlaw/Bublitz_2013.pdf).** Cognitive liberty = "mental self-determination," a right the law "will have to recognize"; the term "has only recently been put forward by US legal scholars and civil rights activists (e.g. Boire 2000; Sententia 2004; Blitz 2010)"; the idea is older, "in the works of ... Kant and Mill." Freedom of thought "is an absolute right, i.e. there are no limitation clauses" and therefore "has to be construed narrowly." **Footnote 23 is the published objection to the draft's central move:** "Blitz (2010) ... proposes that the protection of freedom of thought should be expanded to 'activity that is [...] the functional equivalent of thought' and therewith to computers, IPhones and other devices. However, this expansion eliminates the distinction between personality and property rights. While technical devices / data-storage need (and in fact, enjoy) legal protection, their protection is based on property rights. Even though machines might be functionally similar, freedom of thought can only be meaningfully construed in relation to the human mental realm."
- **Relation to the draft.** The draft cites Bublitz 2025 (l.76) for the *dormancy* thesis and agrees with it. It does not know that the same author has rejected, in print, the proposition that freedom of thought follows function into devices. The draft's reply is actually available in its own text — it disclaims that the medium *is* the mind (l.84) and rests the protection on "what the reading of diaries does to the people who keep them" (l.84), i.e. on the *conditions of thinking* rather than on the metaphysics — but the reply is never addressed to Bublitz, and Bublitz's "property not personality" line is exactly what a hostile human-rights lawyer will say. The Bublitz 2021 essay ("Freedom of Thought as an International Human Right: Elements of a Theory of a Living Right," https://www.chrisbublitz.de/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Bublitz_2021_Freedom-of-Thought-as-a-Human-Right_Elements.pdf) could not be fetched today (server refused); it is the fullest statement of his narrow-scope view and the author should read it before v2.
- **Verdict:** *agrees* on dormancy; *diverges* on scope without saying so; the divergence is the essay's most exposed flank in this community.

### 1.3 Sjors Ligthart, "Reconsidering the absolute nature of the right to freedom of thought," *Human Rights Law Review* 25:3 (2025), https://academic.oup.com/hrlr/article/25/3/ngaf018/8155294 (read)
- **Claim.** The RFoT has three negative freedoms (no impermissible alteration; no forced revelation of unmanifested thoughts; no punishment for thoughts). "Categorical insistence on the absolute nature ... is unpersuasive" once the right must accommodate therapeutic and protective interferences; proposes *implied limitations* (therapeutic alteration for the incompetent; preventing imminent severe harm; emergency disclosure, e.g. locating a kidnap victim) while keeping an absolute *essence* (no punishment for thoughts alone; no forced disclosure of political/moral views; no means that bypass mental autonomy). Digital techniques (facial emotion recognition, eye-tracking, wearables) are within scope. The premise that inner thoughts are "beyond the reach" of the state is "evidently false."
- **Relation to the draft.** The draft leans on GC22's "no limitations whatsoever" (l.74) as if uncontested. Ligthart is the current best statement that it is contested — and, tellingly, his proposed *exceptions* (imminent harm; emergency disclosure) are exactly the categories OpenAI's August 2025 referral policy already operates. The draft's §XII question 1 ("externality specificity") and question 3 ("minimum necessary legibility") are in effect a proposal for how implied limitations on the externalized right should be drawn; the draft would be stronger if it said it was entering *that* debate rather than assuming absoluteness. Ligthart's companion "Absolute Protection of the Mind? On Freedom of Thought and Beyond" (SSRN, June 2025, https://ssrn.com/abstract=5353727) could not be fetched.
- **Verdict:** the draft *diverges* (absolutist rhetoric) from the direction of the specialist literature; see §4′ below.

### 1.4 Susie Alegre — "Rethinking Freedom of Thought for the 21st Century," *EHRLR* (2017; Doughty Street PDF, read in full, https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/sites/default/files/media/document/Rethinking%20Freedom%20of%20Thought%20for%20the%2021st.pdf); *Freedom to Think* (2022, not read; positions confirmed via her 2023 CIGI report with Aaron Shull, read in full, https://www.cigionline.org/documents/2719/Freedom.of.Thought_SpecialReport.Alegre.Shull.pdf)
- **Claim.** The right has "received little attention ... in part because of an assumption that our inner thoughts were beyond reach." Three elements: "the right not to reveal one's thoughts or opinions; the right not to have one's thoughts or opinions manipulated; and the right not to be penalised for one's thoughts." On inference: "as technology develops more complex ways to surveille us and analyse the resulting data, it becomes less clear which thoughts we are offering to the outside world and which are being extracted without our knowledge"; she opens the disclosure section with Moglen's "They own the search box and we put our dreams in it." CIGI 2023: "What thoughts or information about ourselves are we sharing voluntarily, versus involuntarily through others' inferences? ... How are inferences about our inner lives used against us?"; "As powerful generative AI technologies become more prevalent ... the risks and challenges will only become more pressing."
- **Relation to the draft.** Alegre is the best-known public exponent of the position that the *absolute* forum internum reaches digital inference and profiling. The draft's "cognitive legibility" (l.154) is Alegre's "inferences about our inner lives" with a Scott-derived name and an institutional emphasis. The draft *diverges* in two ways worth stating: (i) Alegre's paradigm case is *manipulation* (Cambridge Analytica, news-feed experiments); the draft's is *observation and permission* — a real and defensible difference of emphasis; (ii) Alegre argues *from* absoluteness to strong regulation of private platforms; the draft argues from the same right to a *limit on state architecture*. That inversion is the draft's most original contribution relative to Alegre, and it is invisible because she is never named.
- **Verdict:** *extends* Alegre on the legibility side; *inverts* her on the state/corporation question; must be cited.

### 1.5 Nita Farahany, *The Battle for Your Brain* (2023) and adjacent essays
- **Claim (sources read: Judicature Q&A, https://judicature.duke.edu/articles/the-battle-for-your-brain-a-legal-scholars-argument-for-protecting-brain-data-and-cognitive-liberty/ ; Microsoft "Unlocked" essay "Cultivating cognitive liberty in the age of generative AI," June 19, 2023, https://unlocked.microsoft.com/ai-anthology/nita-farahany/ ; *Time*, June 26, 2023, https://time.com/6289229/cognitive-liberty-human-right/ ; Substack, Mar. 2, 2026, https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/your-brain-everywhere-inside-my-advanced).** Cognitive liberty is "a fundamental human right both to access and change our brains and to be safeguarded against others doing so," with three components: self-determination, mental privacy, and freedom of thought ("an absolute human right, but much narrower ... because it's only about literally what you're thinking"). She *does* address generative AI: the Microsoft essay warns that GPT-4 "can exacerbate biases and distortions" and calls for "rights against mental manipulation"; the Judicature interview notes the coincidence of the book with ChatGPT and the GPT-based semantic decoder. But her AI discussion is about *manipulation and decoding*, not about *chat logs as a cognitive record*; the March 2026 piece is about emotion-recognition and personality inference in hiring/education and proposes the EU AI Act's categorical ban model. Nowhere in the fetched material does she treat LLM conversation as extended cognition or the transcript as a forum-internum object.
- **Relation to the draft.** The draft's subtitle uses her banner term and her book is the reason the term is current. Not citing her is a gap of *manners* more than of argument: the draft's claim (cognition moved outside the skull, not read through it, l.80) is precisely the case she does not make. The draft should cite her once at l.78 as the neurotech exponent and mark the difference; that costs one sentence and pre-empts the obvious reviewer complaint.
- **Verdict:** neighbor, not predecessor; the draft *extends* the term to a case Farahany's framework leaves out.

### 1.6 Wrye Sententia and Richard Glen Boire (CCLE, c. 2000–2004)
- **Claim (via Wikipedia "Cognitive liberty," read, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_liberty ; and Bublitz 2013's quotation of Boire 2000).** "The right of each individual to think independently and autonomously, to use the full power of his or her mind, and to engage in multiple modes of thought"; Sententia 2004 (*Annals NYAS* 1013) sets two principles: no compulsion to use brain-interactive technology or drugs, no prohibition on their use absent harm to others. Boire 2000: "the right to control one's own consciousness is the quintessence of freedom."
- **Relation to the draft.** The coiners' concern is *pharmacological and neural self-determination*; the draft's is *institutional observability of externalized thought*. Same phrase, different object. A one-line acknowledgement ("the phrase was coined for the drug-policy and neurotechnology debates; this essay uses it for…") is enough. The CCLE definition page itself could not be fetched (server closed the connection); the Wikipedia entry and Bublitz's quotation suffice for attribution.

## 4′. The strongest existing counterargument from these strata, and how the essay fares

Three candidates were tested; the first is the strongest.

**(A) The absolutism the draft borrows is unworkable once thought is externalized, and the specialist literature is already abandoning it.** Bublitz 2013: the absolute right "has to be construed narrowly"; extending it to devices "eliminates the distinction between personality and property rights." Ligthart 2025: the premise that thought is beyond reach is "evidently false," "categorical insistence on the absolute nature ... is unpersuasive," and the right needs *implied limitations* for imminent harm and emergency disclosure. Put against the draft: if the externalized forum internum inherits GC22's "no limitations whatsoever" (l.74), then no warrant, no self-harm protocol, no incident record could ever lawfully reach a chat log — a conclusion the draft itself rejects at l.254 ("a provider that already keeps records may be required to keep them for the incidents the rule names") and l.276 ("a provider that answers a lawful subpoena does not constitute it"). So the draft is *not* an absolutist; it is proposing limits. But it never says so, and it opens §III with the absolutist language. The published objection lands squarely on the rhetoric and glances off the substance.

*How the essay fares:* substantively well, rhetorically exposed. The fix is to relocate the right: say that GC22's absoluteness belongs to the unmanifested interior, that the externalized record is a *new object* to which the right's *rationale* (not its unlimited scope) transfers, and that the seven questions of §XII are the draft's proposal for the limitations Ligthart says must be drawn. That turns the strongest objection into the essay's own framework, and it distinguishes the draft from Alegre's absolutism in a way the specialists will respect.

**(B) Chilling effects are empirically contested.** The draft rests §III's mechanism on Penney 2016 (with the honest "no true control group" caveat, l.90). The critical literature: Schauer (1978) called the theory's empirical assumptions "most likely unprovable"; Bedi, "The Myth of the Chilling Effect," 35 Harv. J.L. & Tech. 267 (2021) (read, https://jolt.law.harvard.edu/assets/articlePDFs/v35/Bedi-The-Myth-of-the-Chilling-Effect.pdf), finds in a social-media experiment that chilling "has little to no impact on the content of the message; at most, it subtly alters the specific style or tone"; Büchi, Festic & Latzer, *Big Data & Society* (2022, abstract via search), say existing designs "have not been able to provide robust accounts of actual chilling effects"; and Penney's own 2022 reconceptualization concedes that fear-based theories are "empirically weak" and proposes *social conformity under uncertainty* instead. Marthews & Tucker's Google study is aggregate and its authors call causation unproven.

*How the essay fares:* adequately. It already limits the claim to "changes the expected cost of inquiry" (l.92) and to a *mechanism* rather than a magnitude; Foucault at l.160 is used for exactly the "uncertainty" point Penney 2022 now emphasizes. But it cites only Penney 2016 and Shaheed's paraphrase. It should cite Penney 2022 (which strengthens the draft: conformity-under-uncertainty is *worse* for a medium of private inquiry than fear-of-sanction) and acknowledge Bedi in a clause. Note that Bedi's finding — style not content — is about *public posting*, where self-presentation already governs; it does not transfer cleanly to private questioning, and the draft can say so.

**(C) Extended-mind framing licenses over-broad rights.** Tesink et al. 2024 and Bublitz 2013 fn. 23 make it; Carter & Palermos illustrate it (your laptop as your person). *How the essay fares:* well — l.58–62 is precisely the disclaimer that answers it, and it is a known move (Tesink et al. adopt EMT "for argument's sake" to show how metaphysics drives rights; Blitz 2010 avoids relying on the strong thesis by using "functional equivalent"). The draft should name the objection it is dodging so the dodge is visible as a choice.

Also noted, from the privacy-law side: **(D) "users already treat chatbots as public / voluntarily submitted."** Stein, J. (Jan. 2026) used exactly this against OpenAI's privacy objection. The draft has the answer — OpenAI's own "uniquely private nature of ChatGPT interactions" (Aug. 2025) and Altman's "most personal sh** in their lives" — and should deploy it.

## 7. Reception forecast for these communities

**Neurorights / freedom-of-thought scholars (Bublitz, Ligthart, Ienca, Alegre, Farahany, McCarthy-Jones, the Handbook contributors).** They will recognize the subject as theirs and the draft as an outsider's. Three reactions, in order of likelihood: (i) "Where is Blitz 2010?" — the extended-mind/freedom-of-thought argument is *their* founding article and the draft re-derives it; (ii) "Where is Alegre?" — the inference-from-data point is her book's thesis; (iii) the substantive one: "the author borrows GC22's absoluteness and then proposes limitations without noticing the contradiction" (Bublitz, Ligthart). The draft's defense against (iii) is already in its text (§XII) and needs only to be made explicit. What they will *value*: the developmental-record object (l.88), which is sharper than "profiling"; the five-degree legibility ladder (l.158); and the turn to architecture, which their literature — rights-focused, court-focused — largely lacks. Expect the Handbook/Palgrave crowd to find §§XI–XIV the most useful part and to cite it as "an argument from constitutional design rather than from the right." Farahany's readership will see the subtitle, look for her, and not find her; that is avoidable.

**Privacy-law scholars (Richards, Cohen, Solove, the Fourth Amendment bar, Pfefferkorn, EFF).** Their first question will be the third-party doctrine (§4), and their second will be the chat-log record (§6). A draft that says "anticipatory" in September 2026 to readers who have followed *NYT v. OpenAI*, the Maine warrant, *Heppner*, *Kim*, and *Chatrie* will read as unread on its own subject, and the excellence of the philosophy will not save it with this audience. Conversely, if §III cites the record and §XI names the doctrine, this community will find the draft's *structural* point — that a warrant requirement governs access but not retention, classification, or referral — genuinely useful, because their own literature is fixated on access. Richards will recognize his 2008 argument carried forward; Cohen will notice "modulation" without her name. Solove's "nothing to hide" is implicit at l.156 and could be named.

**Philosophers of mind (Clark, Chalmers, Smart, Clowes, Heersmink, Carter, Palermos, the Tesink group).** The "this essay does not need the strong thesis" move (l.58) is a known and respected move — Blitz makes it with "functional equivalent," Tesink et al. adopt EMT arguendo, Carter & Palermos need the strong thesis and know it. The draft will be read as philosophically literate and correctly modest. Two notes: the draft's description of what LLMs do ("participates, and participates recursively," l.64) is closer to Clark's own 2025 Comment than to the Synthese paper, which is about RAG; and Palermos 2023 already argues from mental privacy to *technical* (not merely legal) protection — the draft's local-inference conclusion — so the draft has an ally it doesn't cite. The extended-mind community will also note that the draft never says what makes an LLM *integrated* (Clark & Chalmers's trust/reliability/availability conditions) and that a one-off ChatGPT query is not Otto's notebook; the "developmental history of a belief" in a *long-lived* assistant (l.88) is the draft's implicit answer and should be made the explicit one.

**The author's own readers, fresh from *The Politics of Visibility* (read, https://sjsebastian.substack.com/p/the-politics-of-visibility).** What the new essay adds: the object shifts from association to deliberation; "behavioral legibility" gets a successor degree; the Church Committee/Foucault/Penney/Shklar apparatus is reused deliberately and briefly (l.90, l.148, l.152, l.160) with cross-references rather than re-argument, which is the right call. Where it repeats: the "capacity precedes regime" method, the Scott epigraph logic, the Shklar-Pettit pairing, and the "design against foreseeable abuse" conclusion are the same instruments applied to a new object; a reader who has both essays will feel §VIII (authoritarian archive) as the most redundant section, since *Visibility* already made the "constitutional not predictive" point about foreign cases. Where it regresses: *Visibility* cited *Carpenter* and *Chatrie*, Zuboff, Balkin, Cohen, and Stoycheff; this essay, on a more legally live subject, cites none of them. Those readers were told they were now "legally literate"; they will notice. What they will find new and strong: §§II–III (the mind outside the skull; the cognitive record), §X (the hard case, argued against interest), and §XII–XIV (the test and the composed structure). The Hugging Face frame is the kind of documented miniature *Visibility* opened with (Operation Puppet Master), and it works the same way.
